newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico tortilla makers threaten gov't plan boycott.
newsitem.headline: Mexico tortilla makers threaten gov't plan boycott.

text.p: Mexican corn tortilla makers are threatening to boycott a government plan that gives free tortillas to the poorest Mexican families, in a new bid to force authorities to raise or remove age-old price supports.

In two or three weeks, tortilla makers could begin to deny the free basic staple via the country's tortibono scheme in an attempt to force the government's hand, the National Corn Flour and Tortilla Producers Chamber president said.
The corn-based pancakes are eaten more widely than bread and handed out free to the poorest of Mexicans who hold tortibonos, plastic credit card-like coupons.

"We hope (the higher price) will come soon, but if not, poor people are going to be without tortillas, because we are not going to hand over kilos of tortillas under this tortilla coupon plan," chamber president Carlos Gonzalez told Reuters.

Tortilla makers have long argued that the government's subsidy is now insufficient to cover production costs, and Gonzalez said the chamber's 37,000 members - 70 percent of the nation's total - have agreed to boycott the tortibono scheme to force higher subsidies or to free prices.

Aside from handing out free tortillas to the poorest Mexicans, the government also sets tortilla prices exaggeratedly low to make sure the entire population has sufficient purchasing power to eat the staple food.
Strict government vigilance of tortilla prices prevents the tortilla makers from charging higher prices.
The decades-old price controls cost the government over $1 billion per year in various subsidies doled out throughout the tortilla chain from corn farmers to corn flour makers.
Tortillas currently sell in Mexico City at controlled prices of 1.70 pesos ($0.22) per kilogram. Outside the capital, prices are also controlled but differ largely depending on corn prices.
Gonzalez said a break-even price would be 2.20 pesos (about $0.28) per kg. Producers are asking for prices of 2.50 pesos (about $0.32) per kg, he added.
"If they stick to the (current) tortilla price, the official price, there will be no tortillas," he said.
Mexico has produced about six million tonnes of tortillas annually for the past two years. The most recent hike in tortilla prices was in December 1996, when prices jumped from 1.40 pesos per kg.
Gonzalez said the tortilla subsidies and the tortibono scheme in particular have been driven by political motives.

"Tortilla prices have been used for electoral ends, and now we see that they are distributing more cards to give away a kilo of tortillas while elections approach, then they will take back all the cards," he added.
In July elections, Mexicans will replace legislators in the lower house of Congress, plus elect the governors of Mexico City and seven other states.
Big gains are expected for opposition parties after almost 70 years of uninterrupted rule by the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI).
